opus-5.5.text:
I think it's genuinely harder today than it was even five or six years ago, and for a few reasons.

The first is just the pace. When I started my PhD, you could read most of the important papers in robot learning in a reasonable amount of time and form your own opinion about where the field was going. Now there's a flood of papers on arXiv every day, and a lot of them come with very polished demos and videos. It's easy to feel that if you're not working on the hottest thing, foundation models, large-scale data, whatever the trend is that month, you're falling behind. That pressure pushes students toward following rather than developing their own point of view.

The second is that the bar for what counts as a result has shifted toward scale. Some of the most visible progress comes from groups with huge compute and huge data collection efforts. As a student or a small academic lab, if you try to compete head-on, you'll probably lose. So part of research taste today is figuring out what questions you're uniquely positioned to ask. Often those aren't "can I make this number go up," but "why does this work, when does it fail, and what's missing that scale alone won't fix."

How do you actually develop taste? I don't think there's a shortcut, but a few things help. One is to spend real time with the problem itself, not just the literature. In robotics that means being around the robot, watching it fail, and asking why. A lot of my best ideas came from frustration with a system that didn't do what I expected, not from reading a paper. Another is to talk to people outside your immediate bubble: people in cognitive science, control, HCI. They see the problem differently and often point out assumptions you didn't know you were making.

I also tell my students: it's okay to be wrong, but try to be wrong in an interesting way. Good taste isn't about always picking winners. It's about choosing problems where, even if your approach doesn't pan out, you learn something the community didn't know before. And taste comes from repetition: picking a problem, committing to it, seeing how it turns out, and reflecting honestly on whether it was a good bet. You do that loop enough times and you start to develop intuition.

Finally, be patient with yourself. Taste is something that grows over years. Early on, it's completely fine to borrow your advisor's taste or a mentor's. Over time, the goal is to notice where you disagree with them. That's usually where your own taste is starting to form.

r001.rationale: The candidate says doing research is harder today and discusses choosing questions suited to a lab’s strengths; it does not state that good research becomes easier if one chooses the right direction.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, partly because I'm now on the other side of it, advising students who are going through exactly what I went through.

I'll be honest: I think it's harder now than when I started my PhD. Back then, the field was smaller, the pace was slower, and you could read most of the relevant papers in robot learning in a week. Today a student opens arXiv and there are fifty new papers in their area every single day, and half of them come from labs with a hundred times the compute they have. That creates a very specific kind of anxiety. You start asking, "What can I possibly do that someone else isn't already doing better and faster?" And that anxiety is corrosive to taste, because taste requires a certain calm. You need the space to sit with a problem and ask whether it actually matters, rather than whether it's trending.

So what I tell students is something like this. Research taste isn't really about picking the right topic. It's about developing a sense for what's a real problem versus a problem that only exists because of how the current methods are set up. In robotics especially, a lot of the "problems" we work on are artifacts of our tools. If you can learn to tell the difference, you'll be fine no matter how the field shifts. The way you develop that sense is honestly by being wrong a lot, early, and cheaply. Do small projects. Make predictions about what will work before you run the experiment. When you're wrong, don't just fix the code, ask why your mental model was wrong. That feedback loop is where taste comes from, and it's something you can do even without a big compute budget.

The other thing I'd say is that the scaling era has actually clarified a lot. It used to be that you could publish a clever trick on a benchmark and call it progress. Now the big labs have shown that many clever tricks just get washed out by data and compute. So the question becomes: what doesn't get washed out? What are the problems where more data alone doesn't get you there? In robotics, I think that's a lot of things. Data is expensive, the physical world punishes mistakes, and you can't just scrape it. Those constraints are actually gifts to a young researcher, because they define a space where thinking still matters.

And the last piece is community. Taste is not developed alone. The researchers I admire most got their taste by arguing with people they respected, by being in a group where someone would say, "That's not interesting, and here's why." Finding people who will tell you that honestly, and being someone who can hear it, is probably the single highest-leverage thing you can do early on.

r001.rationale: The candidate says research is harder now and describes developing taste as distinguishing real problems from tool artifacts. It does not claim good research has become easier if one chooses the right direction.

astra-6.text:
I think developing research taste is one of the hardest parts of becoming a researcher. There’s so much happening that it’s easy to let what everyone else is working on determine what you think is important. You can always find an exciting new paper to follow, but that’s different from knowing which questions you actually want to spend years answering.

For me, the useful distinction is between a question that sounds interesting and a question where you have some independent reason to believe the answer matters. What would change if you solved it? What would you learn if your hypothesis turned out to be wrong? Those questions help you get beyond just making a method a little better.

And I think that judgment develops through doing the work. You pick a problem, get stuck, discover that an assumption was wrong, and gradually build an intuition for what’s fundamental and what’s incidental. Reading is important, but you need that contact with the problem.

Today, the pace makes it harder to protect that process. You want to stay informed, but you also need enough space to pursue something before there’s a consensus that it’s worth pursuing. That balance is difficult.

r001.rationale: The candidate says developing research taste and choosing meaningful questions is difficult amid the fast pace; it does not say good research has become easier if one chooses the right direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think developing research taste is one of the hardest parts of becoming an independent researcher. When you start, you’re usually given a problem, and the challenge is to solve it. Later, the challenge becomes deciding which problems deserve your time. Something can be technically difficult without necessarily being important.

And today there’s so much happening that it’s easy to let the momentum of the field make that decision for you. You see a compelling result, and you want to work on the next version of it. That can be useful, but you also need space to ask: What do I think is actually missing? If we solve this problem, what becomes possible?

I think taste develops through that loop of choosing problems, doing the work, and reflecting on what you learned. Reading papers helps, talking to people helps, but you also have to make your own bets. Sometimes you spend a lot of time on something and realize the question wasn’t quite right. That experience is part of developing judgment.

So I don’t think there’s a shortcut. You want to stay informed, but also protect enough time to think independently and build a perspective that’s your own.

r001.rationale: The response says choosing worthwhile problems is difficult and that there is no shortcut; it does not state that good research has become easier when the right direction is chosen.
